pages: Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving Model Training. Abstract: We study federated learning, a paradigm in which many client devices collaboratively train a shared neural network without transmitting their raw local data to a central server. The research problem is how to learn an accurate global model while keeping sensitive user data on-device, thereby preserving privacy and reducing communication cost.

Introduction and objectives. The main objective of this work is to reduce communication overhead in federated learning while maintaining model accuracy under non-IID data distributions across clients. We also aim to quantify the privacy benefits of keeping data local compared with centralized training.

Methodology. Our proposed method extends Federated Averaging (FedAvg): each client performs several local stochastic gradient descent steps, and the server aggregates the client model updates using a weighted average based on local dataset size. We add gradient clipping and a secure aggregation step so the server never sees an individual client's update in the clear.

Experimental setup. We evaluate on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets partitioned across 100 simulated clients. Evaluation metrics are top-1 classification accuracy, the number of communication rounds to reach a target accuracy, and total bytes transmitted. We compare against centralized training and vanilla FedAvg baselines.

Results. The proposed method reaches 97.1% accuracy on MNIST and 71.4% on CIFAR-10, within two percentage points of centralized training, while reducing communication rounds by roughly 35% compared with vanilla FedAvg. Secure aggregation added modest computational overhead per round.

Limitations and future work. Limitations include degraded convergence under extreme non-IID partitions and the assumption of honest-but-curious clients. Future work will explore robustness to adversarial clients, personalization for heterogeneous devices, and formal differential-privacy guarantees.
